01.note: Rabbi Yitzhak asks Rav Nahman why he has not been coming to the synagogue to pray. Rav Nahman says he is too weak; when Rabbi Yitzhak suggests gathering a prayer group at home, Rav Nahman says it would be too much of a burden on the community. Rabbi Yitzhak then proposes that a messenger tell him when the congregation is praying so he can pray at the same moment. Asked why he is making such a fuss, Rabbi Yitzhak explains with a teaching from Rabbi Yohanan: the 'time of favor' in a verse from Psalms is the time when the congregation prays.
01.why: The Gemara has been quoting teachings of Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai; this exchange introduces another one, on the special power of communal prayer, which the discussion then supports with further verses.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage of the Talmud who presses his colleague to join communal prayer.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, here too weak to come to the synagogue.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A leading Sage of the Land of Israel, whose teaching Rabbi Yitzhak quotes.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: An earlier Sage, the original source of the teaching on communal prayer.

terms.meaning: Communal prayer requires a group of at least ten adult men, called a minyan. Certain prayers can only be said in such a group.
A respectful way the Sages address one another, used in place of 'you'.

02.note: When Rabbi Eliezer's maidservant dies, his students come to comfort him as they would a mourner. He tries to avoid them, going upstairs, then into the gatehouse, then into the banquet hall, and they follow him each time. Finally he scolds them for missing the hint and reminds them of his own teaching: the formal mourning rites are not held for slaves. Instead one says to the owner what one says when an ox or donkey dies, 'May the Omnipresent replenish your loss.'
02.why: The mishna says Rabban Gamliel accepted condolences when his servant Tavi died, and the Gemara has just quoted a teaching that the mourning rites are not observed for slaves; this incident is the source of that teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the Temple's destruction, teacher of many students.

terms.meaning: After a burial, comforters lined up in rows and the mourners passed between them to receive words of comfort.
A special blessing recited in the mourners' presence, part of the formal rites of comforting them.
A name for God, literally 'the Place', used often in words of comfort.

03.note: A student asks Rabbi Yehoshua whether the evening prayer is optional or required and is told 'optional'; Rabban Gamliel, head of the Sages, tells him 'required'. Rabban Gamliel raises the question in the study hall, forces Rabbi Yehoshua to admit his view, and leaves him standing while he lectures. The angry assembly removes Rabban Gamliel and appoints the young Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, whose hair miraculously turns white. The study hall is opened to all students, and Rabban Gamliel keeps attending. Later he visits Rabbi Yehoshua, is shocked to learn he earns his living as a blacksmith, and begs forgiveness. Rabbi Yehoshua forgives him and goes with Rabbi Akiva to help restore him; the story's final arrangement is not given here.
03.why: The mishna says the evening prayer 'is not fixed', and the Gemara has just shown that the Sages disagreed whether it is optional or required; this is the famous dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua on that very question.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Head (Nasi) of the Sages after the Temple's destruction, known for a firm, demanding leadership.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: A leading Sage who holds the evening prayer is optional; poor, he works as a blacksmith.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: A wise, wealthy young Sage, a descendant of Ezra, chosen to replace Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A great Sage from a family of converts; he backs Rabbi Yehoshua and then helps make peace.

people.name: Yehuda, the Ammonite convert
people.about: A convert who asks whether he may marry into the Jewish people.

terms.meaning: The president or head of the Sages and of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
A nickname for the Torah scholars, who 'battle' over the law in the study hall.
A tractate of the Mishna (the early collection of Jewish law) made up of testimonies about earlier rulings.
A priest who sprinkles purifying water and red-heifer ash on the impure; used here as an image for the rightful hereditary leader.

03.flag: The story's ending (the shared leadership arrangement, and the reveal that the student was Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai) sits in the segment right after the story span; the span stops one segment short.

04.note: Mar, son of Ravina, holds a wedding feast for his son and sees that the Sages there are getting carried away with merriment. To sober them, he brings out a valuable cup worth four hundred zuz and breaks it in front of them, and they become sad.
04.why: The discussion is about restraining excessive joy, with Sages rebuking each other for it; this is one of several incidents in which a host deliberately dampens the celebration at a wedding.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, son of the Sage Ravina, hosting his son's wedding.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of the period. Four hundred zuz was a large sum, which is the point of breaking the cup.

05.note: Rav Pappa visits the home of Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan. After the meal is over, more food is brought out and Rav Pappa eats it without saying a new blessing. His hosts ask whether he does not hold that once a meal is finished one may not eat again without a blessing. He answers that the rule as correctly taught speaks of the table being removed, not of finishing the meal.
05.why: The Gemara is discussing which blessings apply to food eaten at the end of a meal; this incident is the first of several about when a meal counts as over, so that eating more needs a new blessing.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, here a guest.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who hosts Rav Pappa.

terms.meaning: In those days food was served on small individual tables, which were carried away when the meal ended. Rav Pappa holds that only then is the meal truly over.

06.note: Giddel bar Manyumi is standing near Rav Nahman when Rav Nahman forgets to add the special Shabbat passage to Grace after Meals. Rav Nahman goes back and says the whole Grace again from the beginning. Asked why, he cites Rav's teaching, as reported by Rabbi Sheila: one who made this mistake goes back to the beginning.
06.why: The Gemara has just reported Rav's ruling that one who forgot the Shabbat passage in Grace after Meals adds a short substitute blessing; this incident gives a conflicting report of Rav, which the discussion then reconciles.

people.name: Giddel bar Manyumi
people.about: A Sage who watches Rav Nahman and questions his practice.

people.name: Rabbi Sheila
people.about: A Sage who reported Rav's ruling.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A founding Sage of Babylonian Talmudic learning, whose rulings are quoted throughout.

terms.meaning: The set of blessings said after eating bread. On Shabbat a special passage is added.

06.flag: The exchange continues in the next segment (Giddel's challenge from Rav Huna's report and Rav Nahman's answer), which falls outside the story span.

07.note: Yehuda bar Natan is walking behind Rav Hamnuna and lets out a sigh. Rav Hamnuna asks whether he wants to bring suffering on himself, quoting Job: 'that which I did fear is come upon me.' Yehuda replies with the verse 'Happy is the man who fears always,' and Rav Hamnuna answers that that verse is about fear of forgetting Torah.
07.why: The mishna calls a frightened prayer about a scream in the city a vain prayer, and the Gemara is praising trust over fear; this incident, like the one before it, teaches that one should fear only for one's Torah learning.

people.name: Yehuda bar Natan
people.about: A Sage, here walking with Rav Hamnuna.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who rebukes his companion for sighing.
